title: Sofacy_Fysbis_Backdoor_Investigation_3c5
description: You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential compromise involving the Sofacy group's Fysbis backdoor on a Linux-based network. The Fysbis malware is known for its remote shell access, persistence mechanisms, and command and control (C2) communication capabilities. Your goal is to identify and mitigate the threat.
outcomes: Identify and investigate suspicious services and processes.
Analyze network communication for signs of C2 activity.
Collect forensic evidence and contain the threat.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential compromise involving the Sofacy group's Fysbis backdoor on a Linux-based network. The Fysbis malware is known for its remote shell access, persistence mechanisms, and command and control (C2) communication capabilities. Your goal is to identify and mitigate the threat.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: Access the target host via SSH using the following credentials: Username: cyrano, Password: cyrano. Enter 'start' to begin.
levels.local_content: Access the target host via SSH using the following credentials: Username: cyrano, Password: cyrano. Enter 'start' to begin.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: While monitoring the network, you noticed unusual outbound connections from the target host. Investigate the target host to identify any unauthorized or suspicious services running.
levels.solution: To identify suspicious services, you can use commands like `systemctl list-units --type=service` or `ps aux` to list all running services and processes. Look for any services that seem out of place or unfamiliar. The hidden flag is the name of the suspicious service.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the list of running services and look for any that seem out of place or unfamiliar.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-units --type=service` or `ps aux` to list all running services and processes.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The suspicious service name starts with 'systemkernel' and ends with '.service'.

levels.title: Persistence Discovery
levels.content: Now that you have identified a suspicious service, determine how it is automatically started after a system reboot. This will help you understand the persistence mechanism used by the attacker.
levels.solution: To identify persistence mechanisms, examine systemd services and timers using commands like `systemctl list-unit-files --type=service` and `systemctl list-timers`. Look for any services or timers related to the suspicious service. The hidden flag is the name of the persistence mechanism or identifier.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Examine systemd services and timers to find any related to the suspicious service.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-unit-files --type=service` and `systemctl list-timers` to identify persistence mechanisms.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The persistence mechanism name starts with 'systemkernel' and ends with '.timer'.

levels.title: C2 Communication Discovery (Port)
levels.content: Investigate the network traffic to determine which port is being used for the suspicious communication between the target host and the potential command-and-control server.
levels.solution: To identify the port used for suspicious communication, use commands like `ss -tulnp` or `netstat -tulnp` to list all network connections and listening ports. Look for any unusual or unexpected ports. The hidden flag is the port number used for the suspicious communication.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the network connections and listen ports to find any unusual or unexpected ports.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use commands like `ss -tulnp` or `netstat -tulnp` to list all network connections and listening ports.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The port number is a common one used for HTTP traffic.
